Djawa Baroe (1943–1945)

When Japanese War Propaganda Sounds So Local

How did the Japanese Empire attempt to sway Indonesian public opinion through mass media during the Second World War?

Research and text: Dwika Resti PutriFirst Cycle · 2026
Begin the exhibition ↓
Indonesia · 1942–1945Magazine & photographic archivePhoto essay
In this exhibition
  1. Occupation & media
  2. Imagined inclusivity
  3. Everyday propaganda
  4. Women & representation
  5. Wartime urgency
  6. Sources & credits
01

An occupation, a magazine, a message

Almost a year after the arrival of the Japanese military in the Dutch East Indies (modern-day Indonesia) on 8 March 1942, Djawa Baroe (modern spelling: Jawa Baru, meaning “New Java”) appeared on 1 January 1943. The bilingual, Japanese state-sponsored propaganda magazine was published fortnightly for Indonesian readers.

After 63 issues, its final edition appeared on 1 August 1945, about two weeks before Japan’s defeat and surrender in the Second World War.

To advance the Greater East Asia Co-Prosperity Sphere, the Japanese Empire used wartime propaganda both at home and in occupied territories. From 1937, nationalist messages increasingly blurred the distinction between the battlefield and domestic life, mobilising people through patriotic images, songs, school materials and other forms of popular media (Yamashita; Kushner).

In the occupied territories, those messages took on local forms. Djawa Baroe presented itself as a “communicative bridge” between Japan and Indonesia, promoting an ideal of Asian brotherhood against what its publishers characterised as Western imperialism. As the Allies advanced and resistance grew, the magazine’s militaristic appeals became more explicit. This project traces that change through the magazine’s visual language from 1943 to 1945.

1942Japanese occupation begins1943First magazine issue1945Final issue and surrender
02

Inclusivity as a gateway

At first, the Japanese Empire portrayed itself as an “older brother” liberating Indonesians from Dutch colonial rule. In place of Dutch influence, the magazine presented a visual language of apparent equality between Japanese and Indonesian people. Its covers invited readers to recognise themselves in scenes of friendliness, leisure and cultural exchange.

Such images were not neutral representations of daily life. They formed part of a political effort to make Japanese occupation appear familiar and desirable.

The first issue, published on 1 January 1943, also devoted a page to a manifesto declaring the magazine’s mission. It described the publication as a meeting place for Japan and Indonesia and promised to communicate the “truth” in support of Japan’s wartime cause. That claim of truth was itself an element of propaganda.

03

The language of everyday life

Djawa Baroe addressed an educated Indonesian readership while promoting Japanese-language learning through short instructional sections. Its pages also carried war songs, comic strips and illustrations situated within recognisable scenes of ordinary life.

Language, entertainment and domestic imagery worked alongside overt political messaging. Through these familiar formats, propaganda entered the spaces of reading, learning, working and family life.

04

The contradictions of women’s representation

Djawa Baroe frequently depicted women and girls in sharply contrasting roles: as military participants and as figures of domestic responsibility. The magazine’s representations of confident, active women stood in stark contrast to the kidnapping and sexual enslavement committed by the Japanese military during the war.

The photographs cannot be read as proof of universal consent or participation. They reveal the version of women’s roles that the occupying authorities wanted the public to see.

Curatorial note · Images and consent

The people shown in these historical images appear within a state-produced propaganda magazine. Their depiction as willing supporters should not be taken as direct evidence of what they believed, whether they consented to being photographed, or how they experienced the occupation.

05

When soft power could no longer contain the urgency

As Japan’s military position worsened, the magazine’s appeals became more direct. The advertisement published on 15 January 1945 ties personal health to the duty to fight for the Japanese Empire, making the demands of total war especially visible.

Earlier issues had also represented influential Indonesian figures, including Sukarno and Mohammad Hatta—later Indonesia’s first president and vice-president—as young anti-Western-imperialist politicians who worked alongside Japan. As Japan’s military situation became more desperate, the tone and purpose of Djawa Baroe shifted.

Censorship remained central to the publication, although, as Putut Widjanarko observes, Indonesians working at the magazine could still encounter uncensored articles and news. Beyond the magazine’s official messages, news of the war and political developments circulated through other channels. On 17 August 1945, two days after Japan’s surrender, the independence of the Republic of Indonesia was proclaimed.

Reading these pages in sequence shows a propaganda strategy that changed over time: from imagined intimacy and “brotherhood” to an increasingly urgent demand for labour, sacrifice and military commitment.

An invitation to look closer
How does propaganda become persuasive when it looks and sounds like the world its readers already know?
The project

Reading images as historical evidence

This exhibition follows the changes in a wartime magazine’s visual and editorial strategies, examining how local aesthetics could carry imperial messaging.

Where & when

Dutch East Indies (present-day Indonesia), during the Japanese occupation of 1942–1945. The magazine was published between January 1943 and August 1945.

Format & method

Historical photo essay and close reading of selected covers, language lessons, songs, comics, photographs and advertisements reproduced from the magazine.

Why the story matters

The familiar appearance of children at play, women at work and people taking part in local cultural life could be used to make imperial occupation appear inclusive. Dwika Resti Putri’s project places that visual language alongside the escalating demands of war. It also asks how initial Indonesian participation in Japanese-sponsored narratives can be remembered alongside nationalist histories, without flattening the complex positions of victims, perpetrators and collaborators.

Documentation

Sources & Credits

Original project research, historical magazine reproductions and bibliographic references. The magazine’s images are included as historical evidence, not as endorsements of the messages they carry.
